subject: botany_2
question_text: Give a brief account of the tools of recombinant DNA technology.

verification.note: Sourced from "Sr. Botany — My Baby Bullet-Q" (Sri Publishers, STAR-Q Pass Track), book p.16, printed question 4. Botany-II holds only ONE source book: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no Telangana Botany-II board paper is in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the board back-test are BOTH structurally impossible for this card — "not checked" does NOT mean "checked and clean". Run both the moment a second source or a real paper arrives. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

insider_note: Five tools. List all five in the first four lines, then take them in turn — an examiner scanning for five headings finds them immediately, and the list alone protects a mark.

steps.label: The five tools
steps.margin_note: All five, numbered, before anything is explained. Six lines.
lines: Recombinant DNA technology uses FIVE tools:
1. Restriction enzymes
2. Polymerase enzymes
3. Ligases
4. Vectors
5. Host organisms
steps.why: Naming all five first turns the rest of the answer into five labelled sections, which is exactly how the marks are split.
common_mistakes: Naming three tools. There are FIVE.
Calling gel electrophoresis a tool. It is a TECHNIQUE used in the process, not one of the five tools.

steps.label: Restriction enzymes
steps.margin_note: Two marks here. Both nuclease types, the palindrome definition, and the EcoRI sequence written on two lines.

lines.text: 1. RESTRICTION ENZYMES belong to a larger
class called NUCLEASES. They are of two kinds:

lines: (i) EXONUCLEASES remove nucleotides from the
ENDS of a DNA molecule.
(ii) ENDONUCLEASES cut at specific positions
WITHIN the DNA.
Each restriction endonuclease recognises a
specific PALINDROMIC sequence.
A palindrome in DNA reads the same on both
strands, in the same 5' to 3' direction.

lines.text: 5'  G A A T T C  3'
3'  C T T A A G  5'

lines: and cuts between G and A on each strand,
leaving STICKY ENDS.
steps.why: Cutting at a palindrome off-centre leaves short single-stranded overhangs on both pieces, and those overhangs are what make the ends sticky.
common_mistakes: Saying EcoRI recognises GAA. It recognises the SIX-base palindrome GAATTC. The guide's VSAQ answer prints the short version, and it is wrong.
Swapping exo- and endonucleases. EXO cuts from the ends, ENDO cuts within.
Not explaining the palindrome. The definition is part of these two marks.
steps.memory_tip: Endo cuts inside; exo nibbles the ends.

steps.label: Polymerase enzymes
steps.margin_note: What it does, the PCR link, Taq, and the billion copies.
lines: 2. POLYMERASE ENZYMES build new DNA strands.
In the POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION, many
copies of the gene of interest are made using PRIMERS
and DNA polymerase.
TAQ POLYMERASE is used because it remains active
at high temperature.
Repeating the cycle about 30 times gives roughly
a BILLION copies.
The amplified fragment can then be ligated into
a vector for cloning.
steps.why: Amplification comes before cloning because a single copy of a gene is too little to work with reliably.
common_mistakes: Saying polymerase joins two DNA molecules. That is LIGASE.
Leaving out Taq polymerase by name. It is the answer to why PCR works.
steps.memory_tip: Polymerase copies; it does not join.

steps.label: Ligases
steps.margin_note: The action, the bond, the product, and the scissors-and-glue pairing.
lines: 3. LIGASES join two pieces of DNA.
DNA LIGASE joins the ends of the plasmid DNA to
the ends of the desired gene by COVALENT bonds.
It regenerates a circular hybrid molecule, the
RECOMBINANT DNA.
Ligase is often called MOLECULAR GLUE, as
restriction enzymes are called molecular
scissors.
steps.why: The sticky ends only hold the two pieces together loosely by base pairing; the covalent bond ligase makes is what turns them into one molecule.
common_mistakes: Saying ligase cuts DNA. It JOINS.
Leaving out the covalent bond. The kind of bond is the point.

steps.label: Vectors
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Definition, examples, then all four properties numbered.
lines: 4. A VECTOR is the DNA used as a CARRIER, to
transfer a fragment of foreign DNA into a
suitable host.
Vectors used to multiply foreign DNA are called
CLONING VECTORS.
Common cloning vectors are PLASMIDS,
BACTERIOPHAGES, COSMIDS, BAC and YAC.
PROPERTIES a cloning vector must have:
(i) LOW molecular weight, so it is easy to
handle;
(ii) a UNIQUE cleavage site for a restriction
enzyme, so it opens at one place only;
(iii) the ability to REPLICATE inside the host
after it is introduced;
(iv) a SELECTABLE MARKER, which identifies and
eliminates the non-transformants.
steps.why: A vector must open at exactly one place, or the gene could be inserted anywhere and the vector might be cut into useless pieces.
common_mistakes: Giving fewer than four properties. All four are expected for two marks.
Leaving out the selectable marker. Without it there is no way to tell which cells took up the vector.
Saying a vector must be large. It must have LOW molecular weight.
steps.memory_tip: Small, one cut site, self-copying, and it flags the cells that took it.

steps.label: Host organisms
steps.margin_note: Definition, the named host, the competence treatment, and one closing list.

lines.text: Cut, copy, join, carry, host: five tools

lines: 5. HOST ORGANISMS are the cells in which the
recombinant DNA is multiplied and expressed.
ESCHERICHIA COLI is the commonest host.
A host is made COMPETENT for transformation by
treating it with divalent calcium (Ca2+) ions,
which makes its wall permeable to DNA.
Yeast and plant and animal cells are also used.
steps.why: A host cell has to be persuaded to let DNA through its wall, and the calcium treatment is the standard way of doing it.
common_mistakes: Saying E. coli is a plasmid. It is a BACTERIUM; its plasmids are the vectors.
Leaving out the calcium treatment. Making the cell competent is what this mark is for.
steps.memory_tip: Calcium makes the wall leaky enough to let DNA in.
